title: Work
subject: Physics

English.simple_explanation: In physics, work is done only when a force actually moves an object.
English.detailed_explanation: Work equals the force applied multiplied by the distance the object moves in the direction of that force: W = F x d. Its SI unit is the joule (J), where one joule is one newton acting through one metre. If the object does not move, or if it moves at right angles to the force, then no work is done in the physics sense, however tiring the effort may feel.
English.everyday_example: Lifting a bag of rice onto a shelf does work on the bag. Standing still while holding that same bag above your head does no work in physics, even though your arms soon ache.

local_example.text: Lifting a filled container onto a raised platform does work on it, because the upward force moves the load upward.
local_example.appropriate_usage: Use as a general local-context draft only until reviewed; do not present it as a claim about any specific household, worker, or place.

common_misconceptions: Any effort that makes you tired counts as work in physics.
Holding a heavy object still does work on it.

observe_around_you.invitation: Find something heavy enough to be a real effort to hold — a full bucket of water works well.
observe_around_you.what_to_do: Hold it still, at arm's length, for as long as you can. Then lift it from the ground up to your chest a few times.
observe_around_you.what_to_notice: Holding it still burns and aches. But the bucket did not move at all. Lifting moves it, and that feels like effort too.
observe_around_you.concept_link: In physics, work is force times the distance moved along that force. Holding still moves nothing, so it is zero work — even though your muscles are clearly labouring. This is the sharpest case where the everyday word and the physics word part ways.
observe_around_you.safety_note: Keep your back straight, lift with your legs, and stop as soon as it hurts.

think_question: You push hard against a wall for a whole minute and it does not move. Your muscles are tired, so how much work have you done on the wall in the physics sense, and why?

reasoning_guide.correct_feedback: Good reasoning: you tied work to the object actually moving, not to how tiring the effort felt.
reasoning_guide.partial_feedback: You are close. State clearly what the wall did or did not do, and what that means for the work done on it.
reasoning_guide.misconception_feedback: Feeling tired is not the test. In physics, work needs the force to move the object through a distance.

challenge.question: A force of 20 N pushes a crate 3 m along the floor in the direction of the force. How much work is done, in joules?
progressive_hints: Substitute 20 for the force and 3 for the distance.
Multiply the two values, then write the unit as J.
challenge.solution: W = F x d = 20 N x 3 m = 60 J.

quiz_questions.question: A 15 N force moves a box 4 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done, in joules?
quiz_questions.explanation: W = F x d = 15 N x 4 m = 60 J.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the force by the distance moved.
progressive_hints: Multiply the force by the distance moved.
Calculate 15 x 4, then give the answer in joules.
